about: Where a thing lives. A producer knows its own URLs and nobody else can guess them, so an address is a value the producer hands over — never a rule a consumer applies. These cases exist because the alternative design is tempting, cheaper, and wrong.

when.importInto: a tool that builds its own links

cases.why: An address is the producer's to state. A consumer that overwrites it with one built from its own routing scheme has turned a working link into one that resolves only inside itself, and every link ever pasted from that consumer points at the wrong library.

when.importInto: a tool that models collections as boards

cases.why: Collections were the last part of the format whose top-level keys had nowhere to land, because every key one could carry was consumed by an exhaustive handler. That handler was exhaustive until `url` arrived, and then a board's address vanished with no finding and no trace. An exhaustive handler fails silently at exactly the moment it stops being exhaustive.

Absent means this producer publishes no address for this thing, which is a different fact from an address that went missing. A consumer that invents one has to guess an origin and interpolate an id, and it will hand somebody a link that goes nowhere while looking exactly like one that works.

Opaque like an id: no stripping query strings, no dropping fragments, no rewriting a path that looks redundant. A producer's routing may need every part of that string, and a consumer cannot tell which parts by looking — the workspace segment here is not decoration.

A template is the cheaper design and it is the wrong one. It is a construction rule, and a consumer holding one will build addresses for objects that never traveled — including objects that do not exist — by parsing and interpolating an id the format says is opaque. One string per object costs bytes. A template costs the id rule. An address a producer hands you is not a licence to construct another one.
